newsitem.title: USA: Arafat must move to end violence - Mordechai.
newsitem.headline: Arafat must move to end violence - Mordechai.

text.p: Israel's defence minister said on Thursday the Middle East peace process could remain stalled unless Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat actively moves to stop violence in and around Israel.

"We have to have back our partner, Chairman Arafat," said Yitzhak Mordechai, who was visiting Washington as the Clinton administration engaged in a new round of contacts to try to halt an escalation of Israeli-Palestinian violence.

"He (Arafat) and his commanders must fight against terrorism and deny all terrorism and all violence in the area. That is necessary for us to take more risk and to move forward with the peace," Mordechai told reporters.

He was speaking at the start of a meeting with U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen and in advance of talks in Washington next Monday between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Bill Clinton.

Negotiations have been derailed by Israel's decision to build new housing for Jews in East Jerusalem, which has provoked Arab outrage and U.S. criticism. Violent clashes and bombings have occurred in the Gaza strip and West Bank.

Mordechai, who was to hold talks later on Thursday with U.S. Secretary of State Medeleine Albright, made clear that Israel had no intention of quickly halting settlement work, especially construction of new housing in East Jerusalem.

When asked if the work might be halted in order to stop bombings and rock-throwing, he said: "I think we have our right to keep Jerusalem united for the Israeli people and for the Palestinians who are living there."

Mordechai added: "There are a lot of subjects that we are discussing with the Palestinians to improve quite a large part of life in the area and, unfortunately, someone doesn't want to continue with us to find a solution."
Clinton met this week in Washington with Jordan's King Hussein and said afterwards that he was willing to make considerable personal effort to rescue the peace process.

King Hussein was reported to have told a small group of reporters after the talks that the current crisis required "a more active U.S. role" and saying: "Minds have to be put to work and heads need to be knocked together."
But the State Department has turned aside questions from reporters on whether a new U.S. role might involve a Middle East summit meeting in the United States.

A landmark peace accord between Israel and Egypt was forged in 1978 in meetings at Camp David, the U.S. presidential retreat in rural Maryland. The United States also helped to broker a string of follow-on Israeli-Arab accords.

Cohen told reporters before his meeting with Mordechai that the two would discuss joint security cooperation, including work on Israel's Arrow anti-missile programme and a U.S.-developed high-energy laser designed to shoot down short-range rockets aimed at Israel.

But he also stressed that Israel's military superiority in the Middle East was only one pillar of Israeli security, adding, "The other pillar is continued progress on the road to a comprehensive peace agreement."
